sources.title: Generative AI and Information Literacy: Academic Integrity and Citation

quotes.text: Before you use any AI tool, ask yourself: Is using this tool in compliance with the course instructor’s standards? Does using this tool undermine your “honest effort” in this course to receive a grade? If you have any doubts, it is best to ask your instructor, and keep in mind that each course may have different standards of what might be acceptable.

If you are permitted to use an AI tool in your work and you have made the decision to use one, it may be a good idea to acknowledge your use as follows: Which tool(s) did you use? How did you use the tool (for what purpose, in what sections, etc.)? How did you prompt the tool? When did you use the tool?

quotes.text: Conversely, the default assumption for any unsupervised (e.g., “take-home”) assessment task is that the use of AI tools is permitted so long as the use is duly acknowledged.

quotes.text: Whether or not using an AI tool in a particular way is allowable depends on the learning purposes of the course and the targeted outcomes of the assignment.

You should thus always assume that the AI’s output is incorrect until you have separately checked it against reliable sources (citing those sources properly) or have gone through the workings yourself.

sources.title: Library Services / Generative AI guidance

quotes.text: Review your department’s current policy on using and disclosing generative AI in academic work.
Unless explicitly authorised, using AI to create assessed work may be treated as an offence such as contract cheating under Imperial’s Plagiarism, Academic Integrity & Exam Offences regulations.
You should include a statement to acknowledge your use of generative AI tools for all assessed work, in accordance with guidelines from your department or course team.
Guard against AI “hallucinations” by fact-checking every statement before use.

sources.title: Generative AI and Academic Integrity
sources.publisher: University of Toronto Mississauga Academic Integrity
sources.scope: UTM campus / student courses; reports University stance

quotes.text: The University of Toronto takes the stance that students are not allowed to use generative AI in a course unless the instructor explicitly permits it.
Use of generative AI tools when not permitted is considered an academic offence and can result in an allegation of academic misconduct being raised by your instructor.
Do not input any private, confidential or identifying information into generative AI.
